growth_story.headline: Curaçao's income per person has drifted down since 2002; a tourism boom since 2021 has made up the pandemic loss but not the old peak.
growth_story.arc: The record shows one long era: income per person peaked in 2002 and shrank by an average of 0.6 percent a year from 2001 to 2024. It fell in all but two years from 2003 to 2019, and the IMF ties a decade of negative growth to a shrinking offshore financial sector and the closure of the oil refinery, which suffered from the crisis in Venezuela. The pandemic then cut income per person by 17.4 percent in 2020, when travel stopped. Since then, growth of 5.2, 7.3, 3.3 and 4.1 percent a year from 2021 to 2024 has come mostly from tourism, which the IMF calls a pivot to a tourism-led growth model. Even so, income per person in 2024 was still 18.8 percent below its 2002 peak and below its level in 2000.

threads.title: Offshore finance and refinery fade
threads.text: For about two decades, Curaçao's old earners shrank. The IMF links a decade of negative growth to the decline of the offshore financial sector and the closure of the oil refinery, which was hit by the crisis in neighbouring Venezuela.

threads.title: The pandemic collapse
threads.text: When travel stopped in the pandemic, income per person fell by 17.4 percent in 2020, the deepest drop in the record. The Netherlands gave liquidity support to help the islands through it.

threads.title: A tourism-led rebound
threads.text: Since 2021, stayover tourists and the building of hotels and holiday homes have driven growth, and income per person rose every year from 2021 to 2024. Tourism has taken the place of refining and offshore finance as the main source of growth.

growth_story.tension: The IMF describes strong expansion since the pandemic, with fast growth in tourist arrivals. The data show that most of this growth won back the 2020 loss: income per person in 2024 was still below its 2018 level, 18.8 percent below the 2002 peak and below 2000. Growth has also come with fewer formal jobs.
